title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive
abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
abstract: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

title: Multi-Branch Transformer
abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

title: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data
abstract: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from 27.79% to 51.38% and its Calmar ratio from 0.955 to 4.043, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of 4.90 on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
abstract: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

title: MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to 3.58times, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.

title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

title: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference. We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/Tideway .

title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

abstract: My world-model fidelity ruler is a whole-frame PSNR / SSIM that stays high when the one moving object is wrong, so it cannot tell me whether the model predicted the thing the task depends on, which is why fidelity and success disagree across my categories: 'Because these metrics are computed over the full frame, they are dominated by static background pixels, hence can remain high even when a small moving object is mispredicted' (sec. title: A leaderboard cost is a measurement with no uncertainty budget: write the GUM budget for one HAL run (replicate draw, cache state, accounting rule, price vector, token reconstruction), sum it in quadrature with the common components cancelled, and ask which accuracy-cost frontier steps are compatible on the cost axis too
abstract: In metrology a reported value is never a point: the measurand is defined, the measurement equation $Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_N)$ lists every input that moves the result including corrections and the conditions of measurement, each input gets a standard uncertainty $u(x_i)$ evaluated either by statistics on repeated observations (Type A) or from an assumed distribution over the information available (Type B, a rectangular interval of half-width $a$ giving $u = a/\sqrt{3}$), the components are combined by the law of propagation of uncertainty $u_c^2(y) = \sum_i (\partial f/\partial x_i)^2 u^2(x_i) + 2\sum_{i<j} (\partial f/\partial x_i)(\partial f/\partial x_j)\, u(x_i, x_j)$, reported as an expanded uncertainty $U = k\,u_c$ with coverage factor $k = 2$ for about 95%, and two results are metrologically compatible when their difference is smaller than a chosen multiple of the standard uncertainty of that difference, which is lower than the root-sum-square when the two share positively correlated components (NIST TN 1297 summary; VIM 2.47). The agent field reports cost as a point. Card 2611.21515 re-prices 333 HAL runs from token logs, finds published costs up to 11.7x the reconstruction (cache tokens counted twice; 16 o3 runs at a stale $10/$40 sheet, 5.0x), says reconstructed costs 'support comparative analysis rather than exact historical invoices', then runs its paired McNemar test on accuracy alone and feeds exact costs into the Pareto frontier and the selection replay; card 2611.22238 writes the bill as $U + cC + pO$, finds the same condition's premium at $+8\%$ (siblings warm the cache), $+36\%$ (own-cache) and $+29\%$ (alone on a fresh server), puts the replicate noise of one 201-task evaluation at 3-4% relative, and never adds the terms. Carried into L1 with L3, the import says: the cost of one leaderboard run is a measurement whose budget has a Type A term (the agent's draw, per-task coefficient of variation 0.3-0.5 from 2608.25399's $\times 1.34$ geometric SD and 2611.22238's 3-4% over 201 tasks, so 5-9% on a 48-task total), a reproducibility term for the cache state (hit rate 0.90-0.98 moves the input bill 1.6x at a tenth-price cache, so about $\pm 20\%$ on the total, $u \approx 0.12$), a bias term for the accounting rule (token-exact versus 784-token-block hits, $+4\%$ to $+58\%$ by tokenizer; provider fields counted twice, 11.7x), a bias term for the price vector (a factor 1.5-1.9 across the current API range $c \in [0.025, 0.1]$, common to every run priced on one sheet and cancelling in same-model differences), and a reconstruction term (run-level cache tokens spread over tasks by prompt share; imputed cells; 42 runs without records). Pre-registered on the SWE-bench Verified Mini frontier of 2611.21515 (34 runs, 48 tasks, $34.16 to $170.78, four Pareto steps, geometric mean step 1.50x): with the rule and the sheet declared, $u_{c,r} \approx 0.14$ per run, the standard uncertainty of a log cost difference about 0.20, and the smallest resolvable cost ratio at $k = 2$ about 1.5x, so two of the four SWE-bench Mini steps and at least twelve of the 35 frontier steps across the seven benchmarks are incompatible on neither axis (judgment 0.45); the field assumes cost is exact and uncertainty lives on accuracy, or that cost noise is a replicate problem more runs fix; belief-changing results are a Type A share above 60% of $u_c^2$ (replicates fix it, the service answer of the killed CL-W43-14 stands) or $u_{c,r}$ under 0.10 (cost is exact enough and the story is the gross-error audit 2611.21515 already wrote). Probe: $0 on the public HAL archive for the price, reconstruction and four-replicate-group terms, about $300-600 of API spend to re-run three cheap configurations under three cache conditions twice each, zero GPU-hours, nine days; kill written.

sentences: A measured quantity $Y$ (the measurand) is 'determined from $N$ other quantities $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N$ through a functional relation $f$, often called the measurement equation', and 'Included among the quantities $X_i$ are corrections (or correction factors), as well as quantities that take into account other sources of variability, such as different observers, instruments, samples, laboratories, and times at which observations are made'; the function 'should express not simply a physical law but a measurement process, and in particular, it should contain all quantities that can contribute a significant uncertainty to the measurement result' (NIST, Essentials of expressing measurement uncertainty, 'Basic definitions', adapted from TN 1297 and the ISO GUM).

Each input's uncertainty is a standard uncertainty $u_i$, 'equal to the positive square root of the estimated variance', evaluated either as 'Type A evaluation: method of evaluation of uncertainty by the statistical analysis of series of observations' or 'Type B evaluation: method of evaluation of uncertainty by means other than the statistical analysis of series of observations', the latter 'obtained from an assumed probability distribution based on all the available information' — for an interval $[a_-, a_+]$ that holds the value with practical certainty and no further information, 'model it by a uniform (i.e., rectangular) probability distribution' with $u_j = a/\sqrt{3}$, $a = (a_+ - a_-)/2$ the half-width (NIST, 'Basic', 'Type B').

The components combine by the law of propagation of uncertainty, $u_c^2(y) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right)^2 u^2(x_i) + 2 \sum_{i<j} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\, u(x_i, x_j)$, 'a first-order Taylor series approximation of the measurement equation' in which the partial derivatives are 'sensitivity coefficients' and $u(x_i, x_j)$ 'is the estimated covariance'; for a product of powers the relative uncertainties add in quadrature, $u_{c,r}^2(y) = a^2 u_r^2(x_1) + b^2 u_r^2(x_2) + \dots$; the result is reported as an expanded uncertainty $U = k\,u_c(y)$ where 'When the normal distribution applies and $u_c$ is a reliable estimate of the standard deviation of $y$, $U = 2 u_c$ (i.e., $k = 2$) defines an interval having a level of confidence of approximately 95%' (NIST, 'Combining', 'Expanded uncertainty'). Two results are compared by metrological compatibility: 'property of a set of measurement results for a specified measurand, such that the absolute value of the difference of any pair of measured quantity values from two different measurement results is smaller than some chosen multiple of the standard measurement uncertainty of that difference', with the note that 'If the measurements are completely uncorrelated, the standard measurement uncertainty of their difference is equal to the root mean square sum of their standard measurement uncertainties, while it is lower for positive covariance or higher for negative covariance' (VIM3 2.47, Note 2).
sources: https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Uncertainty/basic.html, typea.html, typeb.html, combination.html, coverage.html — NIST 'Essentials of expressing measurement uncertainty', adapted from Taylor and Kuyatt, NIST Technical Note 1297, itself based on the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM) (fetched 2026-11-22; measurement equation, Type A / Type B, rectangular rule, law of propagation, coverage factor)
https://jcgm.bipm.org/vim/en/2.47.html — JCGM 200 (VIM3) entry 2.47 'metrological compatibility of measurement results' with Notes 1-2 (fetched 2026-11-22)

import_sentence: In metrology a reported quantity carries an uncertainty budget: the measurement equation lists every input that moves the result, each input gets a standard uncertainty from repeated observations (Type A) or from an assumed distribution over what is known (Type B), the terms are summed in quadrature with sensitivity coefficients and covariances, and two results are called compatible only when their difference exceeds a chosen multiple of the uncertainty of that difference, which shrinks for components the two share; carried into L1 with L3, that says the dollar cost of one agent leaderboard run is a measurement whose equation is 2611.21515's Eq. 1 summed over calls and tasks, whose inputs are the agent's draw (Type A, 5-9% on a 48-task total), the serving cache state at execution (reproducibility, about $\pm 20\%$ at a tenth-price cache), the cache-accounting rule and the price sheet (biases, 4-58% and a factor 1.5-1.9, common to runs priced one way and cancelling in their differences) and the token reconstruction (allocation and imputation), that no fetched source has written this budget or summed it, and that once it is summed the smallest resolvable cost ratio between two runs on one leaderboard is about 1.5x at $k = 2$, which is the geometric mean step of the SWE-bench Verified Mini accuracy-cost frontier, so the frontier's cost axis is as unresolved as 2611.21515 found its accuracy axis to be.

predicts.statement: Setup. Measurand: the complete-run API token cost $C$ of one configuration (model, scaffold, settings) on a fixed task set $T$, at a declared price vector $p$ and under a declared cache condition, as 2611.21515 Eq. 1 defines it per call, $C = \sum_{j \in T} \sum_{\text{calls}} \left[(I - R - W)\,p_I + R\,p_R + W\,p_W + O\,p_O\right]$, with $I$ inclusive input tokens, $R$ cache-read tokens, $W$ cache-write tokens, $O$ output tokens and $p_\cdot$ their prices. Budget rows, each with its evaluation type, its magnitude from the two cards and its sensitivity: (A) replicate draw of the agent, Type A, per-task coefficient of variation 0.3-0.5 (2608.25399: run-to-run geometric SD $\times 1.34$ on token spend; 2611.22238 Table 7: 'relative standard error of one evaluation's mean cost 3-4% (201 tasks, one run each)', which implies a per-task CV of about 0.5), so $u_r^{A} \approx 0.05$-$0.09$ on a 48-task total; (B1) cache state at execution, reproducibility, Type B: the input bill per prompt token is $1 - (1 - c)\,h$ with $c$ the cached price and $h$ the hit rate, so at $c = 0.1$ a hit rate between 0.90 and 0.98 moves the input bill by a factor 1.61 and the total bill by about $\pm 20\%$ (input is 62-81% of the bill at $c = 0.1$, 2611.22238 sec. 2; TraceLab's measured 95.6% hit rate sits inside the range; sibling conditions warming 3.7-6.7% of prompt tokens moved a premium from $+36\%$ to $+8\%$), rectangular half-width 0.20, $u_r^{B1} \approx 0.12$; (B2) cache-accounting rule, bias, Type B: token-exact versus 784-token-block hits changes the input bill by a factor 1.58 for Qwen3.6-27B (9.8% fewer hits) and 1.05 for Qwen3-Coder (0.8%); provider fields counted twice give 11.7x and 9.9x (two Anthropic runs), and the bill with cache ignored versus counted differs by the whole $R(p_I - p_R)$ term; (B3) price vector, bias, Type B: across the current API range $c \in [0.025, 0.1]$ the same token streams bill 1.54-1.90x apart (from 2611.22238's 18-30% cached share of the bill at $c = 0.025$), and a stale sheet gives 5.0x (16 o3 runs); (B4) token reconstruction, Type B: run-level cache tokens allocated to tasks 'proportionally to their prompt-token counts', missing or non-positive cells imputed at the run's median positive cell cost, 42 of 375 extracted runs with no recoverable token record. Covariances: B2 and B3 are common to every run a leaderboard prices by one rule and one sheet, so their covariance across two runs equals their variance and they cancel in a same-sheet difference (VIM 2.47 Note 2); B3 does not cancel across models whose sheets changed on different dates; A and B1 are run-specific and add. Quantities: $u_{c,r}(C)$ for each of the 34 SWE-bench Verified Mini runs; for each adjacent pair $(i, i')$ on each of the seven Pareto frontiers, the compatibility ratio $E = |\ln C_i - \ln C_{i'}| / \left(k\, u(\ln C_i - \ln C_{i'})\right)$ at $k = 2$, resolved on cost iff $E > 1$; the Type A share $u_A^2 / u_c^2$; and the number of frontier steps resolved on accuracy (2611.21515 Table I: 8 of 35), on cost, and on both. P1: with B2 and B3 declared and cancelled, $u_{c,r} \approx \sqrt{0.07^2 + 0.12^2} \approx 0.14$ per run, the standard uncertainty of a log difference about $\sqrt{2} \times 0.14 \approx 0.20$, and the smallest resolvable ratio $e^{2 \times 0.20} \approx 1.5$x; the four SWE-bench Mini frontier steps span $34.16 to $170.78 (geometric mean step 1.50x), so two of four are unresolved on cost and, across the seven benchmarks, at least 12 of 35 steps are unresolved on cost; combined with Table I's 27 of 35 unresolved on accuracy, fewer than 5 of 35 frontier steps are resolved on both axes. P2: the Type A share of $u_c^2$ is under 0.35 (0.25 at the central values), so adding replicates cannot bring the resolvable ratio under 1.3x while the cache condition is undeclared. P3: the four repeated-configuration groups in HAL (2611.21515 sec. VII) show reported-cost differences between replicates larger than their reconstructed-spend differences, as the one replicate the paper discusses does ('substantially different reported costs despite similar reconstructed spend', sec. V-A): the accounting and cache terms exceed the draw term in the only free replicates that exist.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.45 that P1 holds as written (two of four SWE-bench Mini steps and at least 12 of 35 steps unresolved on cost at $k = 2$ with the rule and sheet declared) and P2 holds (Type A share under 0.35); 0.25 that the Type A share exceeds 0.60 because the provider-billed cache state varies less across executions than the local-vLLM sibling experiment suggests (hit rates within $\pm 1$ pp, $u_r^{B1} < 0.04$); 0.30 that $u_{c,r} < 0.10$ once the rule and sheet are fixed, so that only steps under 1.3x are unresolved and the frontier's cost axis is mostly resolved. Expected mechanism: at a tenth-price cache the uncached tokens are a few percent of input, so the bill is a small difference of large numbers and any protocol influence on the hit rate (concurrency, TTL expiry during tool calls, block granularity) is amplified about tenfold into the bill, whereas the agent's draw moves the total over 48 tasks by only its per-task CV divided by about $\sqrt{30}$.
predicts.field_assumes: Three stated positions. (i) Cost is exact and the uncertainty lives on accuracy: 2611.21515 tests accuracy differences with McNemar and BH and uses point costs in the frontier, the affordability cap and the replay ('exact $C_{ij}$ seen before purchase'), and its prescription is 'Agent leaderboards should report accuracy uncertainty alongside execution costs' (sec. VIII) with costs 'reported separately, with task-level token usage, cache accounting, and model pricing preserved for reproducibility' — preserved, not budgeted; HAL and ARC Prize publish cost per task as a point (pressure review 2026-W41). (ii) Cost noise is a replicate problem: 2609.33812 ('resolving the agent differences we observed would take tens to more than a hundred runs of each'; cost 'differed more than twentyfold between two agents on the same model, mostly through the prompt cache', read as a between-agent fact), 2608.25399 ($\times 1.34$ run spread), 2602.07150's lineage; the killed CL-W43-14 (kill report 2026-11-02) found this position in print and found the expected run share of log-cost variance 4-9%, so 'more runs' is the field's and the pipeline's own prior. (iii) Cache effects are a method property, not a measurement uncertainty: 2611.22238 reports the $+8\% / +36\% / +29\%$ triple as a bias to remove by own-cache accounting and states a 3-5% evaluation noise; 2601.06007 reports 41-80% savings from caching strategies across three providers as a design result; 2607.12161 reports billed cost with savings 'small and statistically uncertain' and no components. The field's own standard (GUM) assumes the opposite of all three: every influence on the result is a budget row with a magnitude, and the dominant row decides what to buy more of.
predicts.belief_changing: If P1 and P2 hold, a leaderboard cost number is a reproducibility-limited measurement: its uncertainty does not shrink with runs or tasks until the cache condition is declared the way temperature is, the accuracy-cost frontier has fewer than 5 of 35 resolved steps on both axes, every 'cheaper at matched accuracy' claim under 1.5x on HAL-style data is a tie, and the selection replay of 2611.21515 must carry cost uncertainty into affordability. If the Type A share exceeds 0.60 on provider-billed replicates, cost is a repeatability problem, more runs fix it, the killed CL-W43-14's service answer (a replicate column) was the right one, and this record is a footnote confirming that provider caches are more stable than local vLLM experiments suggest — a result 2611.22238's authors would cite against their own sibling-bias section. If $u_{c,r} < 0.10$ with the rule and sheet fixed, cost is exact enough for frontiers at 1.3x spacing and the only live issue is the gross-error audit (double counting, stale sheets, missing records) that 2611.21515 already wrote; the import is then a checklist, not a paper. If the price-sheet term fails to cancel across models (sheets changed on different dates for the models on one frontier, as the o3 case shows), the cross-model frontier steps carry a further 0.15 each side and the resolvable ratio moves to about 1.8x, which would make the SWE-bench Mini frontier a single resolved step from cheapest to leader.

identifiability: Measurand first (GUM): the budget is for 'the API token cost of configuration $X$ on task set $T$ at declared price vector $p$ and declared cache condition', not for 'the invoice of run $r$'; the invoice is one realization and has no uncertainty, which is why 2611.21515's 11.7x finding is a gross error (a blunder to correct, in metrology's own category) and not a budget row. Random given: fixed configuration, fixed task set (the 48 shared Mini tasks; the 50-of-500 subset choice is a definitional component of 'cost on SWE-bench Verified' and is reported separately, with 2611.21515's 20.4% mid-range bias and 1.69x hard-task cost as its magnitude), fixed price vector, fixed accounting rule; the Type A term then collects the agent's sampling (temperature stated per run from the HAL manifest) and provider output nondeterminism, and the cache-state term collects the serving conditions at execution (concurrency, TTL expiry during tool calls, block granularity of the provider's cache). Whose temperature: the agent's for Type A; a run at temperature 0 does not have zero cost uncertainty, because the cache state is the provider's and not the agent's, so the budget separates a term that vanishes at temperature 0 from one that does not (Gate 0). Property of the thing or of the protocol: A is a property of the agent system under the prices; B1 is a property of the serving protocol and is what the budget makes visible; B2 and B3 are properties of the leaderboard's accounting choices, fixed by declaration and common across its runs, so they enter a same-sheet difference through their covariance and cancel (VIM 2.47 Note 2) and enter a cross-model difference only through the part that is not shared (sheets dated differently). Type B rows are intervals of ignorance about the protocol, not frequencies; GUM treats them as standard deviations by convention and the record says which rows are which. Judge versus verifier: none; every input is a token count or a price. Premise numbers, all fetched and dated: 2611.21515 (arXiv 2026-11-16): 333 runs re-priced, ratio median 1.00, 95th percentile 5.00, maximum 11.7; 34 runs x 48 tasks, $34.16 vs $170.78, 3 of 4 SWE-bench Mini frontier steps and 27 of 35 overall unresolved on accuracy, 42 runs without token records, four repeated-configuration groups, 20.4% mid-range bias, 1.69x hard-task cell cost; 2611.22238 (arXiv 2026-11-17): $+8\% / +36\% / +29\%$ premium under three cache states, 3.7-6.7% of prompt tokens sibling-warmed, 9.8% / 0.8% fewer hits under block granularity, cached reads 94-98% of input tokens, output 19-38% of the bill at $c = 0.1$, cached share 18-30% of the bill at $c = 0.025$, relative SE 3-4% over 201 tasks; 2608.25399 (abstract and the CL-W43-14 kill report): $\times 1.34$ geometric SD; 2606.30560 (abstract): 'high but imperfect prefix cache hit rates', 95.6% per card 2611.22238.

cheapest_probe.design: Step 1 ($0, 3 days): on the public HAL trace archive (huggingface.co/datasets/agent-evals/hal_traces; 2611.21515's data source) for the seven complete benchmark matrices, recompute every run's cost under 2611.21515 Eq. 1 and evaluate at $0 the rows that need no new runs: B3 by re-pricing each run at the sheet in force on its run date and at the latest sheet (the o3 5.0x case is the extreme; the distribution over 333 runs is the row); B4 by comparing run-level-allocated against per-call cache fields where both exist, and by the share of imputed cells per run; B2 by the bill with provider cache fields counted, ignored, and corrected for the two double-counted runs; A by the four repeated-configuration groups (the only free replicates), reported with their reported-cost and reconstructed-cost differences side by side (P3). Step 2 (about $300-600 of API spend, 0 GPU-hours, 4 days): re-run three of the cheapest SWE-bench Verified Mini configurations in the archive (around $34 per complete run; the scaffold code is HAL's) on the 48 shared tasks under three cache conditions, twice each: sequential with no concurrency, 8-way concurrent, and with a forced pause longer than the provider's cache lifetime inserted before each model call after a tool call (kills the prefix for that run), logging per-call cache_read, cache_creation, input and output token fields as the provider reports them; this gives B1 as a measured reproducibility interval on real billing and A as a two-replicate repeatability per condition, with the provider's reported fields as the rule. Step 3 ($0, 2 days): assemble the budget table per run (row, type, magnitude, sensitivity, $u_i$), compute $u_{c,r}$ per run, the log-difference uncertainty with B2 and B3 cancelled for same-sheet pairs and retained for cross-dated pairs, and the compatibility ratio $E$ at $k = 2$ for every adjacent frontier step on the seven benchmarks; report steps resolved on accuracy (from Table I), on cost, on both; report the Type A share of $u_c^2$. Output: a one-page budget per benchmark and the frontier table with two uncertainty axes, in the form a leaderboard can adopt as a column rule (declared sheet date, declared cache condition, $U$ at $k = 2$).
cheapest_probe.dollars: about $300-600 of API spend (3 configurations x 3 cache conditions x 2 replicates x about $34 per complete 48-task run, choosing the cheapest configurations in the archive; $0 for steps 1 and 3)
cheapest_probe.days: 9 days: 3 of archive work, 4 of re-runs and logging, 2 of assembly
cheapest_probe.kills_if: Dead if, with the accounting rule and the price sheet declared and cancelled, the combined relative standard uncertainty of a one-run 48-task cost is under 0.10 on the three re-run configurations and the cache-state row is under 0.05 (the bill is exact enough for frontiers at 1.3x spacing; the only story is the gross-error audit 2611.21515 already published). Dead as a surprise if the Type A share of $u_c^2$ exceeds 0.60 on the provider-billed replicates (replicates fix it; CL-W43-14's service answer stands and this record is a confirming footnote). Dead as a ruler if the compatibility test at $k = 2$ changes the resolution status of fewer than 3 of the 35 frontier steps relative to a cost-exact frontier (every frontier gap is wider than the floor and the budget changes no decision). Parked, not dead, if the HAL archive's per-call cache fields are too sparse to evaluate B2 and B4 on more than half the SWE-bench Mini runs; the re-open trigger is HAL publishing per-call usage fields, and the re-open cost is step 1 again.

consumers.action_changed: Report each cost with a declared price-sheet date, a declared cache condition (concurrency, provider, cache lifetime) and an expanded uncertainty $U$ at $k = 2$; draw the accuracy-cost frontier with compatibility on both axes instead of a point frontier; if the Type A share is large instead, add a replicate count to the cost column.

consumers.class: Agent-selection and evaluation-purchasing authors (2611.21515's successive-halving replay and selection target $Q$; 2610.00651 and 2605.10075's budget allocation; 2609.11987's unresolved billed ordering)

consumers.class: Cost-method authors (2611.22238's masking and evidence premiums, 2607.12161's token-reduction tools, TokenPilot, AgentDiet, TokenEconomizer 2610.22732's 18-31% savings, 2603.23525's 27.9% saving)

papers.title: Harness or Model? Isolating the Harness Effect in Agentic Coding with a Contamination-Controlled Private Suite
papers.trick: Run the same model under a vendor harness and a neutral one on a private 256-task suite with task-bootstrap intervals, re-price from per-turn usage at frozen list prices, and find the success contrast unresolved and the cost ordering unresolved because 58 runs left no usage record.
papers.did_not_do: The one fetched source that treats a cost ordering as unresolved does it for a single budget row: 'allocating that spend to either cell would move the Opus ratio between 0.7 and 2.3, so the billed ordering is unresolved' (abstract) is a Type B interval for missing usage records, and the paper 'corrects an August 2026 manuscript whose cost figures rested on a usage-semantics defect in our own telemetry' — a gross error of the 2611.21515 kind. It writes no measurement equation, no replicate row (one run per cell: 'These are observed-usage estimates'), no cache-state row, no price-sheet row, no quadrature sum and no compatibility test; the tasks are private and no leaderboard frontier is graded.

papers.title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
papers.trick: Bill agent runs as uncached plus discounted cached input plus output on more than 20,000 logged runs; deleting an old tool output re-bills the whole suffix once, so observation masking that saves 19-25% undiscounted costs 87-116% more at a tenth-price cache.
papers.did_not_do: Holds every row of the budget separately and sums none: the sibling-cache effect ($+8\%$ server-reported vs $+36\%$ own-cache vs $+29\%$ alone) is treated as a bias to remove by own-cache accounting, not as a reproducibility interval on a reported cost; the replicate noise is stated as 3-4% relative SE per evaluation and 4-5% between two evaluations (Table 7) without the cache or price rows beside it; block-granular hit counting (9.8% / 0.8% fewer hits) is an audit, not a row; the price vector is a reference by declaration ('not measurements of a provider's billing system'); the six-point checklist of App. O lists the biases with no magnitudes summed and no uncertainty attached to any cost number; nothing is applied to a leaderboard frontier. Third: 2611.21515 reconstructs 333 HAL costs, finds the gross errors (11.7x cache double count, 5.0x stale sheet), writes 'Reconstructed costs rely on standardized pricing, cache-allocation assumptions, and occasional imputation' and 'support comparative analysis rather than exact historical invoices', then tests accuracy only and uses exact costs in the frontier and the replay; its four repeated-configuration groups are never used for a cost replicate estimate. Fourth: 2609.33812 prices 584 runs 'including the prompt cache' and finds within-cell cost swings (2.2-fold median, 4.6-fold extreme, per the CL-W43-14 kill report) and a twentyfold between-agent gap 'mostly through the prompt cache', one task, no decomposition of the swing into draw versus cache state. Fifth: 2601.06007 measures caching strategies across three providers (41-80% cost savings, provider-specific discrepancies) as a design result for production, never as the uncertainty of a benchmark's reported cost. Sixth: 2607.12161 meters provider-billed cost and finds cache creation and reads dominate input cost with savings 'small and statistically uncertain', no rows. Pre-window precedents with their tricks: the GUM (ISO 1993, JCGM 100:2008) itself, the Type A / Type B budget and $U = k u_c$; ISO 5725 and gauge R&R, repeatability versus reproducibility versus bias as components of one reported value (imported for agent scores in W42 S7xF9 — 2610.00651, 2608.11323 — and for the compactor in W45 S3xF9, both as random-effects designs on scores, never on a cost with Type B rows).

nearest_existing_use.verdict: Not in print. Every row of the budget exists somewhere in the fetched sources as a separate finding — replicate spread of cost (2608.25399, 2609.33812, 2611.22238 Table 7), cache-state sensitivity (2611.22238's sibling triple, 2601.06007's provider strategies), accounting-rule and price-sheet errors (2611.21515's 11.7x and 5.0x; 2609.11987's telemetry defect), missing-record intervals (2609.11987's 0.7-2.3) — and no source writes the measurement equation, classifies the rows as Type A or Type B, sums them in quadrature with the common rows cancelled in differences, attaches $U$ to a leaderboard cost, or tests frontier steps for compatibility on the cost axis; the metrology vocabulary returns zero agent-cost hits (Q1). It is not a rename of the killed CL-W43-14 / W43 S6xF1 record: that record asked for the random-effects share of cost variance (Type A rows only: run, task, harness) and died because the field already said run noise is smaller than task sampling (kill report 2026-11-02: run share 4-9%); this record's dominant rows are Type B protocol terms (cache state, accounting rule, price sheet) that no replicate estimates and no number of runs shrinks, its surprise is that the cost axis of a published frontier is as unresolved as the accuracy axis, and its consequence is a declared condition and an expanded uncertainty, not a replicate column. It is not a rename of the W42 S7xF9 or W45 S3xF9 gauge R&R imports (scores and summaries as random-effects designs). Two-year density: 93 hits over three content queries, about six adjacent papers in twelve months and none on the budget; the two card papers landed 2026-11-16 and 2026-11-17 and both name the missing piece in their limitation text, so the race window is open from both the solo position (public archive, API dollars) and the lab position (HAL's owners can add the column on their own logs).

reason_for_pick: S6 is this week's live L1 shape through two cards that each measure one half of what a cost number is worth: 2611.21515 (HAL re-priced from token logs; 40.1% of SWE-bench Mini pairs and 27 of 35 frontier steps unresolved on accuracy; costs off by up to 11.7x; one run per configuration; costs treated as exact in every test) and 2611.22238 (the bill as $U + cC + pO$; the same premium at $+8\%$, $+36\%$ and $+29\%$ under three cache states; 3-4% replicate noise; a bias checklist with nothing summed). F9's metrology half is the field whose whole business is listing such rows and summing them; its gauge R&R half is spent (W42 S7xF9 for scores, W45 S3xF9 for the compactor), its survival half is spent (W42, W45, W46), and the GUM budget with Type B rows had never been carried into any lane. The W43 S6xF1 import of G-theory onto cost was killed (CL-W43-14, Gate 2B) because its rows were all Type A and the field already knew run noise was small; the open question was whether the protocol rows the cards now quantify dominate, which is a different claim with a different consequence. The arithmetic is Jacob's to check by hand (a difference of large numbers amplifying a hit-rate error tenfold; quadrature with cancellation of common rows).

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2611.21515 sec. VII ('Reconstructed costs rely on standardized pricing, cache-allocation assumptions, and occasional imputation'; costs 'support comparative analysis rather than exact historical invoices or future deployment quotes') and sec. VIII ('Agent leaderboards should report accuracy uncertainty alongside execution costs'; costs 'with task-level token usage, cache accounting, and model pricing preserved for reproducibility'); 2611.22238 Limitations ('Prices are applied to recorded token streams rather than measured from API invoices. The cache accounting approximates within-run reuse and does not reproduce provider-specific expiration, write charges, breakpoints or load-dependent eviction') and sec. 7 ('Whether a prefix stays cached also depends on concurrent agents'); 2609.11987 ('so the billed ordering is unresolved'); 2607.12161 (savings 'small and statistically uncertain'). Who pays: every leaderboard with a cost column; every team selecting an agent under a budget on those columns; every cost-method paper claiming a premium under 1.5x.

relevance.jacob_edge: Direct: an uncertainty budget is the physicist's native instrument; the amplification identity (input bill per token $1 - (1 - c) h$, so $\partial \ln(\text{bill}) / \partial h = -(1-c)/(1 - (1-c)h) \approx -9$ at $c = 0.1$, $h = 0.95$) and the covariance cancellation are napkin checks; no learned component anywhere.

kill_probe.step: Steps 1-3: archive re-pricing for the price, reconstruction and four-replicate rows at $0; three cheap SWE-bench Mini configurations re-run under three cache conditions twice each with provider-reported cache fields; budget table, $u_{c,r}$ per run, compatibility ratio $E$ at $k = 2$ per frontier step, Type A share.
kill_probe.criterion: dead if $u_{c,r} < 0.10$ and the cache-state row under 0.05 with rule and sheet fixed; dead as a surprise if the Type A share exceeds 0.60; dead as a ruler if fewer than 3 of 35 frontier steps change resolution status; parked if per-call cache fields cover under half the SWE-bench Mini runs

scorecard.density_and_ownership: Occupied: the gross-error audit of HAL costs and the reconstruction formula (2611.21515, Nov 2026); the three-stream bill, the sibling-cache bias, the block-granularity audit and the bias checklist (2611.22238, Nov 2026); replicate cost spread (2608.25399, 2609.33812, 2602.07150's lineage; the killed CL-W43-14 record); caching-strategy savings across providers (2601.06007); missing-record cost intervals (2609.11987); gauge R&R for scores (2610.00651, 2608.11323) and for the compactor (W45 S3xF9, killed as in print). Unoccupied in every fetched source: the measurement equation with Type A and Type B rows for a cost number, the quadrature sum with common-row cancellation, $U$ on a leaderboard cost, compatibility of frontier steps on the cost axis, and the Type A share that decides whether to buy replicates or declare conditions. Natural first movers: the 2611.21515 authors (they hold the re-priced archive and name the gap), HAL's owners (they hold the logs and the column), the 2611.22238 group at Huawei (they hold 20,000 runs and the checklist). Re-open test: ask them. Race window: six adjacent papers in twelve months in this sub-shape and two in the last week; a nine-day probe against a window estimated at two to three months; proper-shaped solo, golden only from the lab position with HAL's column.
scorecard.why_now: 2611.21515 (2026-11-16) put the public HAL archive's costs, token fields and frontier in one re-priced table and named 'cache-allocation assumptions', 'standardized pricing' and 'occasional imputation' as the unquantified terms, with four repeated-configuration groups as free replicates; 2611.22238 (2026-11-17) measured the cache-state and block-granularity rows and the replicate row on 20,000 runs and left them unsummed; TraceLab (2606.30560, June 2026) gave the production hit rate (95.6%) that fixes the centre of the cache-state interval; provider cache lifetimes and per-call cache fields have been in the billing APIs since 2025, so the step-2 re-runs log the rule the leaderboard uses.
scorecard.register_and_what_it_is_not: Measurement register with a mechanism (the bill is a small difference of large numbers at a tenth-price cache, so protocol influences on the hit rate are amplified about tenfold while the agent's draw averages out over tasks) and a consequence each way (declare the cache condition and report $U$; or add replicates; or leave cost as a point and keep the audit). It is not a new cost model, not a caching strategy, not a re-run of the gross-error audit, not the random-effects decomposition of the killed CL-W43-14, and not a claim that leaderboard costs are wrong — it is a claim about how far apart two of them must be before anyone can say one is cheaper.

triage_reason: import filed: the dollar cost of a leaderboard run is a measurement whose GUM budget (Type A draw, Type B cache state, accounting rule, price sheet, reconstruction) nobody has written or summed; pre-registered on 2611.21515's SWE-bench Mini frontier that the cost axis is unresolved at about 1.5x once the rows are summed, so fewer than 5 of 35 frontier steps are resolved on both axes; serves cards 2611.21515 (costs treated as exact; four free replicates unused) and 2611.22238 (every row measured, none summed)
