title: The user simulator is a DIF group, not a difficulty shift: on the tau2-bench voice board the same five agents run under the gpt-4.1 and the gpt-5.5 user simulator move by -10 to +16 points around a +7 mean and reorder (Kendall tau 0.20-0.60), so the rank-moving quantity is the agent-by-simulator interaction, which the fidelity indices of 2611.24892 do not measure and the two released-matrix designs (tau2-bench paired submissions, Sim2Real's real-user group) can estimate above a rerun floor
abstract: In psychometrics, 'does this item behave differently for two groups' is answered by differential item functioning (DIF): compare only examinees matched on the measured ability, and call an unmatched difference in pass rate 'impact', not bias (Holland and Thayer 1988); a matched difference is uniform DIF when it is the same at every ability (a difficulty shift) and nonuniform DIF when it changes with ability (the item-by-group-by-ability interaction), measured per item by the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio over ability strata or by a logistic regression with a group-by-ability term. Carried into L1 with the user simulator as the group and the agent as the examinee: the agent sits in both groups, so matching is exact and no ability stratum is needed, a design classical DIF never has. Then the 'easy mode' of a cooperative simulator (Sim2Real 2603.11245: success inflated above the human baseline; Lost in Simulation 2601.17087: up to 9 points across user LLMs) is impact: a shift $\lambda_g$ every agent receives, harmless to a ranking. The quantity that moves a leaderboard is the agent-by-simulator term $\gamma_{ag}$, the sum over tasks of per-task nonuniform DIF, and no population fidelity index (the card's level 2 and 3, the User-Sim Index, CUE's aggregate calibration) contains it, which is why 2611.24892 Table 4 finds the simulator with the lowest fidelity (SimulatorArena on gpt-5-mini, 79 / 74) has the highest ranking agreement ($\tau = 0.67$) and the most faithful (Sonnet 5, 87 / 83) the lowest ($\tau = 0.44$): the indices grade $\lambda_g$ and the task-level term $\delta_{ig}$, the ranking grades $\gamma_{ag}$, and the paper reports both without the decomposition. The import is identifiable today at $0: the tau2-bench voice-v1 board (taubench.com; manifest read 2026-11-22) carries five agents (phonic-1, pine-voice-preview, gpt-live-1-diamond-alpha, ava-zero, gpt-realtime-2) each submitted under the standard user simulator (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, temperature 0.0) and under a gpt-5.5 user simulator, 278 tasks, one trial, per-task rewards in the public S3 bucket; computed here: mean shift +6.4 / +6.8 / +7.5 points (airline / retail / telecom), per-agent shift spread 14.0 / 12.3 / 25.9 points (telecom: pine-voice -10.1, ava-zero and gpt-realtime-2 +15.8), Kendall $\tau$ between the two simulators' agent orderings 0.60 / 0.20 / 0.60, pine-voice from 4th to 1st in retail; per-task discordance 0.07-0.33 against a within-simulator rerun floor of 0.196 (gpt-5 text agent, gpt-4.1 user, retail, 4 trials, 6 pairs 0.158-0.219), so the single-trial standard error of a domain shift is about $\sqrt{0.2/114} = 4.2$ points and the telecom spread is about 4.4 standard errors of a difference of two shifts while airline and retail spreads sit within two. Pre-registered on this and an owned text rerun arm: the rank-moving share $\rho$ (between-agent variance of the shift above the rerun floor, over the total) is between 0.3 and 0.7 (judgment 0.45); the field's user-simulator literature assumes $\rho \approx 0$ (fidelity as population distance, the simulator as a configuration constant, 1.x board rows mixing gpt-4.1 and gpt-5.2 user simulators); $\rho \ge 0.7$ in two domains makes the simulator a rank-moving factor the size of a model generation and every board that lets it vary across rows a non-equated comparison (judgment 0.25); $\rho < 0.1$ kills the import (judgment 0.30). Probe: step 1 the free reanalysis, step 2 four text agents (two open-weight on one H100, two API) under two user simulators with four trials on airline and retail, about 20 GPU-hours and $350, 9 days, solo.

sentences: Differential item functioning (DIF) 'is a statistical property of a test item that indicates how likely it is for individuals from distinct groups, possessing similar abilities, to respond differently to the item'; the null is $f(Y = 1 \mid \theta, G = r) = f(Y = 1 \mid \theta, G = f)$ with $Y$ the item response, $\theta$ the latent ability, $G$ the group, $r$ the reference and $f$ the focal group, and 'it is generally agreed upon in the measurement literature that differences on $Y$ conditional on group membership alone is inadequate for establishing bias' because an unmatched difference $p(Y = 1 \mid G = g) \ne p(Y = 1)$ mixes the groups' ability difference with the item (Wikipedia, 'Differential item functioning', citing the NCME glossary, Camilli 2006, Holland and Wainer 1993, Ackerman 1992).

Holland and Thayer (1988, ETS / ERIC ED272577) make the matching the definition: 'Basic to all modern approaches to the study of dif is the notion of comparing only comparable members of F and R', where 'if both examinee ability and item characteristics are confounded by simply measuring the difference in the performance on an item between unmatched reference and focal group members, the result is a measure of impact rather than of differential item performance'; the statistic is the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio over matched sets $k$, $\alpha_{MH} = \frac{\sum_k A_k D_k / N_k}{\sum_k B_k C_k / N_k}$ with $A_k, B_k$ the reference group's correct and incorrect counts, $C_k, D_k$ the focal group's, $N_k$ the set size, read as 'the average factor by which the odds that a member of R is correct on the studied item exceeds the corresponding odds for a comparable member of F', reported on the ETS delta scale as $\mathrm{MH}_{D\text{-}DIF} = -2.35 \ln \alpha_{MH}$.

Two kinds: 'uniform DIF, where one group consistently has an advantage over the other, and nonuniform DIF, where the advantage varies based on the individual's ability level'; in item-response terms uniform DIF is equal discrimination with shifted difficulty ($a_r = a_f$, $b_r 
e b_f$) and nonuniform DIF is crossing item characteristic curves ($a_r 
e a_f$); the logistic-regression test fits $\mathrm{logit}\, P(Y = 1) =  eta_0 +  eta_1 M +  eta_2 G +  eta_3 M G$ with $M$ the matching score and $G$ the group, where $ eta_2 
e 0$ is uniform DIF and 'if there is a nonzero interaction parameter, this is an indication of nonuniform DIF' (Swaminathan and Rogers 1990, as summarized in the same article).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_item_functioning (raw wikitext fetched 2026-11-22; definition, the two kinds, the impact-versus-DIF paragraph, the Mantel-Haenszel table and common odds ratio, the logistic-regression form)

https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED272577.pdf — Holland, P. W. and Thayer, D. T., 'Differential Item Performance and the Mantel-Haenszel Procedure', ETS 1986/1988 (PDF fetched 2026-11-22; the comparability sentence, the impact paragraph, the odds-ratio reading)

import_sentence: In psychometrics, 'does this item behave differently for two groups' is solved by DIF: compare only ability-matched examinees, call an unmatched pass-rate difference impact rather than bias, and split a matched difference into uniform (a difficulty shift at every ability) and nonuniform (an advantage that changes with ability); carried into L1 with the user simulator as the group and the agent as an examinee who sits in both groups, that says a simulator's 'easy mode' is impact, a shift every agent receives that leaves a leaderboard's order intact, while the quantity that reorders agents is the agent-by-simulator interaction $\gamma_{ag}$, the per-task nonuniform DIF summed over tasks, which no population fidelity index contains, so 2611.24892's finding that ranking agreement and fidelity disagree in direction across six simulators (Table 4) is the expected reading of two instruments grading two different terms, and $\gamma_{ag}$ is estimable now from the five same-agent pairs on the tau2-bench voice board, where the simulator swap's per-agent shift spreads 14-26 points around a 7-point mean and reorders the agents.

predicts.statement: Setting. Agents $a \in \mathcal{A}$, tasks $i \in \mathcal{I}$, simulator groups $g \in \{r, f\}$ ($r$ the reference: real users where a real-user run exists, else the board's standard simulator; $f$ the focal simulator), trials $t = 1, \dots, m$; pass indicator $y_{a i g t} \in \{0, 1\}$ and pass probability $p_{a i g} = \mathbb{E}[y_{a i g t}]$ estimated by $\hat p_{a i g} = m^{-1} \sum_t y_{a i g t}$. Decomposition on the logit scale with sum-to-zero side conditions: $$\mathrm{logit}\, p_{a i g} = \theta_a - b_i + \lambda_g + \delta_{i g} + \gamma_{a g} + \epsilon_{a i g},$$ with $\theta_a$ agent ability, $b_i$ task difficulty, $\lambda_g$ the simulator's main effect (impact: the 'easy mode' shift), $\delta_{i g}$ the task-by-simulator term (uniform DIF of task $i$ under $g$: the simulator makes task $i$ easier for every agent beyond $\lambda_g$), $\gamma_{a g}$ the agent-by-simulator term (the simulator's favour toward agent $a$ across tasks) and $\epsilon_{a i g}$ the three-way residual (per-task nonuniform DIF). The leaderboard column under $g$ is $S_{a g} = |\mathcal{I}|^{-1} \sum_i p_{a i g}$; the simulator swap's displacement of agent $a$ is $\Delta_a = S_{a f} - S_{a r}$; its mean over agents $\bar\Delta$ is the impact, and $\Delta_a - \bar\Delta$ is the rank-moving part (on the probability scale it is $\gamma_{a f} - \gamma_{a r}$ plus the task-averaged $\epsilon$, to first order). Per-task DIF with the agent as the matched set (exact matching, $N_a = 2m$): $$\alpha_{\mathrm{MH}, i} = \frac{\sum_a A_{a i} D_{a i} / N_a}{\sum_a B_{a i} C_{a i} / N_a},$$ where $A_{a i}$ and $B_{a i}$ are agent $a$'s passes and fails on task $i$ under $r$, $C_{a i}$ and $D_{a i}$ under $f$; at $m = 1$ this reduces to the ratio of agents that pass only under $r$ to agents that pass only under $f$, McNemar's discordant counts. Nonuniform DIF per task: $\mathrm{logit}\, P(y_{a i g} = 1) = \beta_{0 i} + \beta_{1 i} \theta_a^{(-i)} + \beta_{2 i} G + \beta_{3 i} \theta_a^{(-i)} G$, with $\theta_a^{(-i)}$ the agent's reference-group score excluding task $i$ (purified matching) and $\beta_{3 i} \ne 0$ the nonuniform term. Noise floor: $\sigma_0^2$, the variance of $\Delta_a$ computed between two trials of the same simulator (a group compared with itself), and $d_0$, the per-task discordance between two same-simulator trials. The rank-moving share is $$\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Var}_a(\Delta_a) - \sigma_0^2}{\mathrm{Var}_a(\Delta_a)}.$$ Data already computed (2026-11-22, tau2-bench voice-v1, one trial, standard simulator gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 at temperature 0.0 versus gpt-5.5-2026-04-23 reasoning xhigh; ava-zero's focal run labelled user-sim v1.1 on openai/gpt-5.5): $\Delta_a$ in points, airline (50 tasks) phonic-1 +10.0, gpt-live-1 -4.0, pine-voice +10.0, ava-zero +8.0, gpt-realtime-2 +8.0, $\bar\Delta = +6.4$, spread 14.0; retail (114) +3.5, +5.3, +14.9, +7.9, +2.6, $\bar\Delta = +6.8$, spread 12.3; telecom (114; pine 109) +3.5, +12.3, -10.1, +15.8, +15.8, $\bar\Delta = +7.5$, spread 25.9. Kendall $\tau$ between the two simulators' orderings of the five agents 0.60 / 0.20 / 0.60; retail order under gpt-4.1: gpt-live-1, phonic-1, ava-zero, pine-voice, gpt-realtime-2; under gpt-5.5: pine-voice, gpt-live-1, ava-zero, phonic-1, gpt-realtime-2. Per-task discordance 0.07-0.33 (retail 0.27-0.33 for all five agents). Rerun floor from the only multi-trial release opened: gpt-5 text agent, gpt-4.1 user at temperature 0.0, retail, 4 trials, discordance over the 6 trial pairs 0.158-0.219, mean $d_0 = 0.196$, so the single-trial standard error of a 114-task $\Delta_a$ is about $\sqrt{d_0 / 114} = 4.2$ points (6.3 at 50 tasks) and $\sigma_0 \approx 4.2$ points; the telecom spread is about 4.4 standard errors of a difference of two shifts, airline and retail about 1.6 and 1.9. Per-task sign agreement across the five agents: tasks where every agent gains under gpt-5.5, 0 / 1 / 0 (airline / retail / telecom); tasks where one agent gains and another loses, 5 / 28 / 13. P1 (rank-moving share): $\rho \ge 0.3$ in at least two of the three voice domains once $\sigma_0$ is taken from a voice rerun (step 2 of the probe estimates it in text; a voice floor needs one same-simulator rerun of one agent, 278 calls). P2 (task-level uniform DIF): the variance of $\ln \alpha_{\mathrm{MH}, i}$ across tasks exceeds its split-half null (the same statistic between two trials of one simulator) by a factor of at least 2 in retail. P3 (the card's disagreement): for the simulators of 2611.24892 Table 4, the population fidelity levels 2 and 3 correlate with $|\lambda_g|$ and not with $\mathrm{Var}_a(\gamma_{a g})$, which is what the level-1 Kendall $\tau$ tracks; testable only if the 9-agent-by-6-simulator per-session matrix is released (location not in the paper), so P3 is a prediction on request, not part of the probe.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.45 that $\rho$ lands in $[0.3, 0.7)$ in at least two voice domains and in the owned text arm (the simulator swap is at least a third interaction); 0.25 that $\rho \ge 0.7$ in two domains (the telecom spread, 4.4 standard errors on the text floor, is the strongest single reading and retail's $\tau = 0.20$ the second); 0.30 that $\rho < 0.3$ everywhere once the voice floor is measured (voice runs carry audio channel effects, frame drops and vocal tics drawn per call, so the voice rerun discordance is plausibly above the text floor of 0.196, and airline and retail spreads are within two standard errors now). Expected mechanism for the interaction: the gpt-5.5 simulator discloses information at a different rate and tolerates a different silence and repetition pattern than the gpt-4.1 simulator (the v1.0 guidelines instruct 'make the agent work for information' and 'if the agent continues to not respond after 2 check-ins, show signs of frustration and end the call'), so agents whose failure mode is a disclosure stall gain and agents whose failure mode is over-talking lose; pine-voice's telecom -10.1 against +15.8 for two others is the candidate case to read first. P2 expected to hold at a factor of 2-4 in retail (28 mixed-sign tasks of 114 on five agents against 1 all-gain task).
predicts.field_assumes: Three stated positions, each with the quantity it measures. (i) Fidelity is a population distance: Sim2Real 2603.11245 introduces the User-Sim Index 'to quantify how well LLM simulators resemble real user interactive behaviors and feedback' and reports an 'easy mode that inflates agent success rates above the human baseline'; 2611.24892's levels 2 and 3 are distribution overlaps and per-trace preservation scores and its own text says 'A level score is an evaluation index, not a calibrated probability of fidelity' (sec. 5.4); CUE 2610.02460 defines outcome calibration as 'agreement with observed success rates and failure patterns when real users interact with the same agent', one agent at a time. All of these are $\lambda_g$ and $\delta_{i g}$: impact and uniform DIF. (ii) The simulator's effect is a shift: Lost in Simulation 2601.17087 reports 'agent success rates varying up to 9 percentage points across different user LLMs' and a miscalibration by task difficulty band, both statements about marginal rates with no agent-matched contrast. (iii) The simulator is a configuration constant: tau2-bench's submission rules say 'Use one agent model and one user simulator, with identical arguments, for every domain and cell' and route a non-default simulator to a 'custom' tab, while the 1.x text board's rows carry gpt-4.1 (gpt-5, 2025-08-09) and gpt-5.2 (gpt-5.5 and Claude Opus 5 banking, 2026) as user simulators on the same board, which assumes the scalar level of measurement invariance (equal intercepts across groups license comparing means) that nobody has tested; and the card's own protocol varies the simulator across six systems and reads the ranking agreement as a property of the simulator alone. The field's (psychometrics') own assumption is the opposite: an unmatched group difference is impact and says nothing about bias until the matched, per-item contrast is run.
predicts.belief_changing: If $\rho \ge 0.7$ in two domains (P1 strong), the user simulator is a rank-moving factor of the size of a model generation (a 26-point spread in telecom against generation gaps of 5-15 points on the same board), the fidelity program is grading the harmless component, every board or model card that lets the simulator vary across rows is comparing non-equated scores, and the recipe consequence is a DIF table per simulator pair (which agents the switch favoured, by how much, above the rerun floor) published with every default change, starting with tau2-bench 2.0's switch of the voice default to gpt-5.5 and its persona block. If $\rho \in [0.3, 0.7)$, the same consequence holds for the default change and the mixed-simulator board, and fidelity indices need the interaction term beside them. If $\rho < 0.1$ after the voice floor (all spread is single-trial noise), the simulator is a uniform shift, 'easy mode' is a harmless intercept, Table 4's disagreement is sampling noise on nine agents, and the import dies: the population-fidelity program is then measuring the only quantity that matters. If P2 fails while P1 holds (agents move, tasks do not), the interaction is a whole-conversation style effect rather than task-specific, which points the simulator-fidelity authors at persona and disclosure rate rather than at task content. A second belief at stake: the pass^k convention (tau-bench's reliability metric) is computed within one simulator and has never been read as a DIF floor; if $d_0$ is 0.2 at one trial, every single-trial cross-simulator comparison in print (the five voice pairs, model cards) carries a 4-6 point standard error per agent that no board prints.

identifiability: Random given: the frozen task frames (tau2-bench voice-v1, canonical task ids with SHA-256 of the task pack, identical across both runs of each pair), the agent as submitted (the same submission day for phonic-1, gpt-live-1 and pine-voice; five days apart for gpt-realtime-2; 27 days apart for ava-zero, which is flagged: an agent update between the runs would enter $\Delta_a$ as a simulator effect, so ava-zero is reported separately), the harness version (tau2-bench 2.0.0 for the Phonic and Avartha pairs, 1.0.0 for gpt-realtime-2, both on the voice-v1 frame), the TTS provider (ElevenLabs eleven_v3), the voice seed (300 in both groups), and the simulator as the one changed factor (user LLM gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 versus gpt-5.5-2026-04-23 at reasoning xhigh; ava-zero's focal run is labelled user-sim v1.1, a possibly different simulator prompt, flagged). Whose temperature: the standard simulator runs at temperature 0.0 by the harness (`llm_args: {temperature: 0.0}` in every v1.0 results file opened), and gpt-5.5 is a reasoning model with no temperature argument, so the simulator's decision variance is pinned near zero by construction and the group assignment is a fixed treatment, not a second sampling party (the 2026-11-08 checklist lesson); the trial coin is the agent's sampling plus the audio channel (frame drops at 1%, background noise bursts at one per minute, vocal tics and non-directed phrases at 0.7 per minute, muffling at 0.2 probability, all drawn per call) plus any API nondeterminism; the rerun floor $d_0$ measures exactly this coin and it is what the one-trial board does not report. Floor status: the text floor (0.196) is from a different agent and modality and is a lower bound for voice; a voice floor needs one same-simulator rerun (no two same-agent, same-simulator voice submissions exist on the board; the two gpt-realtime-2 submissions five days apart are the gpt-4.1 / gpt-5.5 pair). Whose property: $\gamma_{a g}$ is a property of the (agent, simulator) pair, so a ranking under simulator $g$ is valid for real users only if $\gamma_{a g} - \gamma_{a, \mathrm{human}}$ is constant in $a$, and $\lambda_g$ is a protocol constant that no ranking consumer needs; the headline names the shipped levels (gpt-4.1 at temperature 0 versus gpt-5.5 xhigh, both with the v1.0 voice guidelines) because a share depends on which simulators are in the crossed set (the 2026-11-01 lesson). Judge versus verifier: the tau2 reward is a programmatic database-state and action check plus a communicate check that is a substring match in 1.x and a 'semantic' LLM judge (gpt-5.5 at low reasoning, prompt communicate-semantic-v1) in the 2.0 voice files, so part of the voice reward is judged; the probe's text arm runs under 1.x-style programmatic checks and reports the voice results with the judged component separated (reward_breakdown is in each simulation record). Single-group design: the examinee is in both groups, so no matching variable, no purification circularity and no impact confound exist; the price is that the agent's ability $\theta_a$ is estimated from the same tasks, which the purified score $\theta_a^{(-i)}$ handles for the per-task test. Power: five agents give $\mathrm{Var}_a(\Delta_a)$ four degrees of freedom, so P1 on the free data is a reading, and the owned arm adds agents and trials; per-task MH over five agents at one trial has no power per task and is reported as a distribution against its split-half null (P2), never as a per-task verdict.

probe.design: Step 1 ($0, 2 days): the five paired voice submissions already downloaded (results.json per cell from s3://sierra-tau-bench-public/submissions/<name>/trajectories/) plus the gpt-5 4-trial text files (airline, retail, telecom) for the floor; compute $\Delta_a$, $\bar\Delta$, $\mathrm{Var}_a(\Delta_a)$, Kendall $\tau$ with a task bootstrap, the $\ln \alpha_{\mathrm{MH}, i}$ distribution and its split-half null, and separate the judged communicate component of the 2.0 voice rewards; open the pine-voice telecom transcripts where it loses to read the mechanism. Step 2 (about 20 GPU-hours, about $350, 5 days): tau2-bench text, airline (50) and retail (114), four agents (Qwen3-30B-A3B and gpt-oss-120b on one H100 under vLLM; gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-5-mini via API), two user simulators (gpt-4.1 at temperature 0, the 1.x default, and gpt-5-mini or gpt-5.5 at low reasoning), $m = 4$ trials: $164 \times 4 \times 2 \times 4 = 5{,}248$ simulations, user-simulator API cost about $0.04-0.08 each, agent API cost for the two API agents about $0.05 each; this arm measures $d_0$ and $\sigma_0^2$ directly (trials of one simulator), $\gamma_{a g}$ over four agents with intervals, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{MH}, i}$ at $m = 4$. Step 3 (1 day): a voice floor, one same-simulator rerun of one open voice stack is not feasible solo; instead request one rerun from Phonic or Avartha (both submitted pairs within a day) and, failing that, report the voice results against the text floor as a lower bound. Step 4 (1 day): the DIF table per simulator pair (agent rows, $\Delta_a$ with intervals, flagged tasks), written as the artifact a board would publish with a default change.
probe.dollars: about $70 at H100 spot rates plus about $280 of user-simulator and API-agent calls; $0 for step 1
probe.days: 9 days: 2 of reanalysis, 1 of harness, 4 of runs and analysis for the text arm, 1 for the voice-floor request, 1 for the table
probe.kills_if: Dead as a claim if $\rho < 0.1$ in every domain of the text arm (four agents, four trials) and the voice spreads fall within two standard errors of the text floor once the floor is replaced by the voice rerun or by the text arm's own $d_0$ (the simulator is a uniform shift; 'easy mode' is an intercept; the fidelity program measures the quantity that matters), or if the per-task $\ln \alpha_{\mathrm{MH}, i}$ variance in the text arm at $m = 4$ is within 1.5 times its split-half null while P1 also fails. Dead as a ruler if $d_0$ exceeds 0.35 in the text arm (single-trial boards cannot carry any per-agent simulator contrast and the table needs $m \ge 8$, which changes the cost by a factor of 2 and is reported as such). Parked, not dead, if P1 holds in voice at face value but the voice floor cannot be obtained (the finding stands on a lower-bound floor and waits for one rerun). The ava-zero pair is excluded from the kill decision because its runs are 27 days apart under a differently labelled simulator.

papers.title: Lost in Simulation: LLM-Simulated Users are Unreliable Proxies for Human Users in Agentic Evaluations
papers.trick: Run tau-bench retail with real people in four countries and several simulated-user LLMs, and show agent success moves up to 9 points with the user LLM, is overestimated on medium tasks and underestimated on hard ones, and is a worse proxy for AAVE and Indian English speakers.
papers.did_not_do: Every reported quantity is a marginal rate or a difficulty-band calibration: the 9-point range is $\lambda_g$ across user LLMs, the band miscalibration is $\delta_{i g}$ aggregated by difficulty against the human group, and the population result is DIF with the human population as the group and the simulator fixed; no agent-matched contrast, no per-task odds ratio over agents, no separation of the agent-by-simulator term from the shift, and no statement about whether the agents' order changes with the user LLM. It has the design's two ingredients (a real-user group, several simulators) and does not run the matched test.

papers.title: Are Near-Tied LLM Rankings Robust to Family-DIF-Guided Benchmark Recomposition?
papers.trick: Identify items with low differential functioning across model families on one half of a benchmark and rescore the other half on them, finding that 31-47% of near-tied cross-family orderings reverse while global rankings barely move.
papers.did_not_do: The DIF machinery is in print for LLM benchmarks with the examinee's family as the group and the stimulus fixed, on 'static, primarily closed-form' benchmarks (its Limitations); the group here is the test's own stimulus (the simulator), the examinee sits in both groups so no ability matching or purification is needed, the response is a Bernoulli draw with a rerun floor the static setting lacks, and the consequence is a board's cross-simulator comparability rather than item recomposition. Third: 2611.24892 (the card) measures six simulators on 351 sessions and nine agents and reports ranking agreement (Kendall $\tau$ 0.44-0.67) and population fidelity moving in opposite directions (Table 4) with no decomposition and no release location for the matrix. Fourth: 2610.02460 CUE defines outcome calibration at the task-user-pair level for 'the same agent' on tau2-bench, one agent at a time, a $\delta_{i g}$ against real users with no agent axis. Fifth: 2611.21095 SWE-WhatIf ranks five coding agents and finds 'the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents', an agent-by-user-condition interaction observed and not decomposed or floored. Sixth: 2603.11245 Sim2Real runs 451 humans on 165 tau-bench tasks against 31 simulators with a population index, the reference group this import would use, with no per-agent matched contrast. Seventh, the vocabulary neighbour: 2604.00594 decomposes agent ability into LLM and scaffold components under IRT with no simulator facet.

nearest.verdict: filed: the DIF import is made for LLM benchmarks with model family as the group (2609.00482) and with the human population as the group (2601.17087), and the simulator's effect is measured as a shift or a population distance in every fetched simulator paper; no source uses the simulator as the DIF group with the agent as an exactly matched examinee, separates the rank-moving agent-by-simulator term from the shift, or floors it with a rerun, and none has opened the five same-agent simulator pairs on the tau2-bench voice board (per-agent shifts -10 to +16 around +7; $\tau$ 0.20-0.60), computed here for the first time. It differs from the W44 S5xF2 record (version-to-version equating with population invariance by scaffold and model family: two forms, examinee groups, a link function and REMSD against a split-half floor) in group, form and quantity: one form, the stimulus as the group, the same examinees in both groups, a per-item matched odds ratio and an agent-by-simulator interaction, on a board (tau2 voice) the W44 record did not touch. It is not a rename of 2611.24892's level-1 ranking agreement (a $\tau$ against a reference with no decomposition and no floor) nor of Sim2Real's 'easy mode' (impact). title: A depth label is a reading of a (task x model x cap x run) design, not a property of the task: the G-study of the turn-cap depth estimate $D$ of 2611.01927, the index of dependability $\Phi$ for its deep / shallow cut, the one-sided nested model facet the released audit cannot identify, and the Neyman rule for how many runs at the boundary caps and how many models certify a depth label
abstract:
In generalizability theory one observation of an object (here a task) under one condition of each facet (measuring model, turn cap, run, harness) is decomposed by a random-effects analysis of variance into a universe-score component for the object and one component per facet and interaction; a decision study divides each component by the number of conditions it will be averaged over; the generalizability coefficient $Eho^2$ grades relative decisions (ranking tasks) and the index of dependability $\Phi$ grades absolute decisions (a label compared to a cut score), and $\Phi$ counts every component except the object's, main effects included (Brennan 1992, ITEMS module 14). A facet observed under one condition for every object is fixed: its interaction with the object is counted as universe-score variance, and a nested design confounds the components it does not cross (Brennan, Eqs. 14-15). Carried into L1 and onto this week's card: the depth label of 2611.01927 is $D_	au = \min_m D_{	au m}$ with $D_{	au m} = \min\{T \in \mathcal{T} : \max_{r \le 2} X_{	au m T r} = 1\}$, where $X_{	au m T r}$ is the pass bit of task $	au$ under model $m$, stated cap $T$ and run $r$. Writing $y_{	au m k} = \log_2 D^{(k)}_{	au m}$ for the $k$-th independent replicate of the whole capped protocol, the G-study model is $$y_{	au m k} = \mu + 
u_	au + 
u_m + 
u_{	au m} + \epsilon_{	au m k},$$ with $\sigma^2(	au)$ the task's depth (the only part the paper's title claims), $\sigma^2(m)$ a model's general merging ability, $\sigma^2(	au m)$ 'this model fails to merge on this task', and $\sigma^2(\epsilon)$ the protocol residual (both runs failing at a sufficient cap, serving and timing nondeterminism). For a label averaged over $n_m$ models and $n_k$ replicates, $$\sigma^2(\delta) =  rac{\sigma^2(	au m)}{n_m} +  rac{\sigma^2(\epsilon)}{n_m n_k}, \qquad \sigma^2(\Delta) = \sigma^2(\delta) +  rac{\sigma^2(m)}{n_m},$$ $Eho^2 = \sigma^2(	au)/(\sigma^2(	au) + \sigma^2(\delta))$ and $\Phi = \sigma^2(	au)/(\sigma^2(	au) + \sigma^2(\Delta))$. The paper's uses of $D$ ('94% of solved synthetic tasks have $D \le 3$'; 'deep' means $D \ge 5$; its own dataset is sold by median $D = 40$) are cut-score decisions, so $\Phi$, not a rank correlation, is their reliability. The released audit identifies none of the four components: the run facet has no replicate of the label (the second run is skipped once the first passes; caps at or above the uncapped turn count are not run), so $\sigma^2(\epsilon)$ sits inside $\sigma^2(	au m)$; the model facet is nested one-sidedly (GLM-5.3-Flash runs only below DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's estimate and only on tasks with $D > 1$), so $D_{\mathrm{GLM}} > D_{\mathrm{DS}}$ is unobservable and $\sigma^2(	au m)$ has only its lower tail; the harness (terminus-2, 30-minute limit, 10,000-byte output cut, the appended cap text) and the single start state $e_0$ are hidden fixed facets whose interactions with the task are counted as task depth; and 333 of 734 sampled tasks have no label, missing in proportion to the object. The paper's own one-sided numbers size the model facet: the second model lowers $D$ on 40 of 160 existing tasks with $D > 1$ (25%), and of the 40 existing tasks with $D_{\mathrm{DS}} \ge 5$ it brings 11 (28%) below the deep cut; its Spearman 0.91 between the one-model and two-model labels is a part-whole correlation (the two labels share the DeepSeek reading on 361 of 401 tasks and 241 are pinned at the floor $D = 1$), not a reliability. The min over models is an extreme statistic, not a mean: adding a model lowers the label, never raises it, so the published $D$ is biased upward by an amount the D-study rescaling $\sigma^2(	au m)/n_m$ does not describe, and a universe-min label cannot be certified by a small panel (at the observed rate 0.25 per model, three further models still miss an existing lowering with probability $0.75^3 = 0.42$); the field's fix is to declare the model panel a fixed facet and report 'depth for this panel' with $\Phi$. Neyman allocation says where replicates go: the strata are the cells $(	au, m, T)$ with within-cell standard deviation $S = \sqrt{p(1-p)}$ ($p$ the per-run pass probability) and run cost $c_T \propto T$, so $n \propto S / \sqrt{c_T}$ puts zero runs at caps where $p \in \{0, 1\}$ and all of them at the boundary pair ($D^-$, the grid level below the label, and $D$), favouring the cheaper lower cap by $1/\sqrt{2}$; to keep the probability that a label is one level too high under 0.1 for any task whose true pass probability at $D^-$ is at least 0.3 needs $n_r \ge \lceil \ln 0.1 / \ln 0.7 ceil = 7$ runs at $D^-$, where the paper's two runs certify only $p \ge 0.68$. Nobody has computed a reliability coefficient for an agent-task difficulty or horizon label: 2512.06710's ICC is for scores with the query as object; 2610.12466 and 2608.00355 fit item-response difficulties to METR data under the assumption that difficulty is the task's; 2604.00594 decomposes ability, not difficulty. Probe: 60 solved tasks in three depth strata, 4 cheap models of different families, all 8 caps, 4 runs per cell (7,680 capped runs, about $1,000 of API calls, 0 GPU-hours, 7 days); pre-registered with the card's numbers.

sentences: Generalizability theory decomposes one observed score in a crossed design of an object $p$ by facets $T$ and $R$ into variance components for $p$, $T$, $R$ and their interactions, and a decision study divides each component by the number of conditions of the facets it contains; two kinds of error then exist: 'Absolute error is simply the difference between a person's observed and universe scores', $\Delta_p = X_{pTR} - \mu_p$, whose variance $\sigma^2(\Delta)$ 'is the sum of all the variance components except $\sigma^2(p)$', and relative error $\sigma^2(\delta)$, which 'involves fewer variance components', so 'relative interpretations about persons' scores are less error prone than absolute interpretations' (Brennan 1992, ITEMS module 14, pp. 29-30).

Two coefficients follow: the generalizability coefficient $E\rho^2 = \sigma^2(\tau)/[\sigma^2(\tau) + \sigma^2(\delta)]$ for relative decisions and 'an index of dependability that is denoted $\Phi$', $\Phi = \sigma^2(\tau)/[\sigma^2(\tau) + \sigma^2(\Delta)]$ (Eq. 12), which 'is generally less than' $E\rho^2$ and 'is appropriate when scores are given absolute interpretations, as in domain-referenced or criterion-referenced situations' (Brennan, p. 30); the Wikipedia summary states the same split, 'an absolute, or criterion-referenced, decision would be when an individual's test score is compared to a cut-off score', and 'the type of decision that the researcher is interested in will determine which formula should be used' (Wikipedia, 'Generalizability theory', fetched 2026-11-22).

Design decides what is identifiable: with a fixed facet $T$ 'the universe of generalization is restricted' and the estimated universe-score variance becomes $\hat\sigma^2(\tau) = \hat\sigma^2(p) + \hat\sigma^2(pT)$, so the coefficient rises because 'generalizations to narrow universes are less error prone', but 'an investigator cannot logically draw inferences about what would happen if different prompts were used' (Brennan, p. 31); in a nested $p \times (R{:}T)$ design 'independent estimates of $\sigma^2(r)$ and $\sigma^2(tr)$ are needed for the D study, but they are completely confounded in the $\sigma^2(r{:}t)$ G study variance component, and independent estimates of $\sigma^2(pr)$ and $\sigma^2(ptr)$ are completely confounded in $\sigma^2(pr{:}t)$' (Eqs. 14-15, p. 32), and Brennan notes that 'the distinction between a G and D study is blurred, usually because the only available data are for an operational administration of an actual measurement procedure' (p. 32), which is what a released audit is. Where to spend replicates: in stratified sampling 'optimum allocation (or disproportionate allocation)' makes 'the sampling fraction of each stratum proportionate to both the proportion and the standard deviation of the distribution of the variable', so 'larger samples are taken in the strata with the greatest variability to generate the least possible overall sampling variance. Neyman allocation is a strategy of this type', and 'both mean and variance can be corrected for disproportionate sampling costs' (Wikipedia, 'Stratified sampling', fetched 2026-11-22); with cost $c_h$ per unit in stratum $h$ and within-stratum standard deviation $S_h$ the rule is $n_h \propto N_h S_h / \sqrt{c_h}$ (Osier, Survey data in Economics and Finance, sec. 3.3.3, as fetched for the W43 S8xF1 record).

import_sentence: In experimental design and generalizability theory, 'is this label a property of the thing or of the way I read it' is answered by a G-study that treats every condition of the reading (model, cap, run, harness) as a facet, estimates one variance component per facet and interaction, grades a cut-score label by the index of dependability $\Phi$ (which charges every component but the object's), declares a facet observed at one level a fixed facet whose interaction is silently counted as the object's, and spends replicates by Neyman's rule on the cells with the largest within-cell spread per unit cost; carried into L1 and onto 2611.01927, that says the depth label $D$ of a terminal task is a reading of a (task x measuring model x cap x run) design in which the task component $\sigma^2(\tau)$ has never been separated from the model-by-task component $\sigma^2(\tau m)$ (the paper's own one-sided check moves 25% of labels above the floor and 28% of its 'deep' existing labels across the deep cut with one extra model) or from the run residual $\sigma^2(\epsilon)$ (no replicate of the label exists), that the min over two models is an upward-biased extreme statistic no small panel certifies, so a depth label must name its panel as a fixed facet and carry $\Phi$, and that certifying a label to within one grid level takes about seven runs at the cap below the label, not two.

predicts.statement: Setup: 60 solved tasks in three strata by the released label, 20 at $D_{\mathrm{DS}} \le 3$ from the audited public sets (TB2, TW, RST, FACET), 20 at $5 \le D_{\mathrm{DS}} \le 20$ (all 40 such existing tasks are candidates; 11 of the paper's own at 10-20), 20 at $D_{\mathrm{DS}} \ge 40$ from the paper's own set (40 of its 54 solved tasks; if the dataset is not released, the deep stratum is RST and TB2 tasks with $D \ge 5$ and the stratum sizes are reported). Panel of $n_m = 4$ cheap models of different families run in terminus-2 with the paper's limits: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash (the paper's two), MiMo-V2.6-Flash and one Qwen3.5 model at the same price class, serving provider fixed, sampling temperature pinned and reported. Fully crossed over the paper's caps $\mathcal{T} = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80\}$ with $n_r = 4$ runs per (task, model, cap) cell: 7,680 capped runs. From the pass table each (task, model) pair yields two independent paper-protocol labels $D^{(1)}_{\tau m}, D^{(2)}_{\tau m}$ (runs 1-2 and runs 3-4 as the 'up to two runs' pair), a four-model min, and per-cell pass probabilities $\hat p_{\tau m T}$. Quantities: the four variance components of $y = \log_2 D$ ($> 80$ coded one level above 80; a (task, model) pair with no pass at any cap is a censored cell, counted and excluded, with the censoring rate per stratum reported), estimated by the usual mean-square equations within each stratum and pooled; $E\rho^2$ and $\Phi$ for the released design ($n_m = 1$, $n_k = 1$) and for the paper's two-model min; label agreement $A = \Pr[D^{(1)}_{\tau m} = D^{(2)}_{\tau m}]$ per stratum (test-retest of the label); the cut-crossing share $C$ = fraction of tasks with $D_{\mathrm{DS}} \ge 5$ whose four-model min is below 5; the lowering share $L$ = fraction of tasks whose four-model min is below the two-model min, against the paper's 25%. P1 (component ordering above the floor): in the two deep strata $\sigma^2(\tau m) + \sigma^2(\epsilon) > \sigma^2(\tau)$, so $\Phi < 0.5$ for a single-model two-run label. P2 (floor): in the $D \le 3$ stratum $\Phi \ge 0.8$, because the grid floor pins the label (241 of 401 solved existing tasks have $D = 1$, which no model can lower). P3 (extreme statistic): $L \ge 0.3$ and $C \ge 0.4$ (the paper's one extra model gave 0.25 and 0.28; two more models of different families push both up). P4 (run residual): $A < 0.7$ in the $D \ge 40$ stratum, where one grid level is a factor of two and both-runs-fail at a sufficient cap has probability $(1 - p)^2$. Reported alongside: $\hat p_{\tau m T}$ curves per task, the number of runs at $D^-$ needed for a 0.9 certificate per stratum, and the cost per certified label.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.45 that P1, P2 and P3 all hold, so that depth labels are dependable exactly where they are uninformative (the floor, where the paper's '94% have $D \le 3$' stands) and panel-dependent where the paper's own dataset lives (median $D = 40$ becomes 'median 40 for this panel'); the mechanism is that a turn under a stated cap is spent either because the task forces an observation or because this model did not batch, and the second cause is model-specific, so it lands in $\sigma^2(\tau m)$ and is largest on the long tasks where there are the most turns to fail to merge. Probability 0.30 for the field's cell and 0.25 for the belief-changing cell below. Probability 0.5 for P4 on its own.
predicts.field_assumes: The paper treats $D$ as a task label with a model caveat and no component: 'Unlike the idealized $D^*$, $D$ depends on the models, the harness and the single state $e_0$, so it is an estimate rather than a bound' (sec. 2), then audits datasets by '$D \le 3$' shares, calls its own tasks 'deep' by $D \ge 40$, and reads the one-sided second-model check as agreement ('the two estimates order tasks alike: the Spearman correlation of $D$ with the estimate of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash alone is 0.91 over the 401 solved existing tasks', App. E.1), a correlation in which the two labels share one reading on 361 of 401 tasks and 241 are pinned at $D = 1$. The item-response community assumes difficulty is the task's: 2604.00594 fits 'a novel decomposition of agent ability into LLM and scaffold ability components' with difficulty on the item, and 2608.00355 reproduces METR's hard-task shift with 'a single Rasch model with rising ability'. The field's cell, probability 0.30: $\Phi \ge 0.8$ in every stratum, $A \ge 0.85$, $L \le 0.1$ and $C \le 0.15$, the model facet confined to one grid level as in the paper's 32 of 40; then the import is a service (report $\Phi$ and the panel) and not a paper.
predicts.belief_changing: Probability 0.25: the run residual, not the model-by-task interaction, is the largest component above the floor, $\sigma^2(\epsilon) > \sigma^2(\tau)$ with $A < 0.5$ in the $D \ge 40$ stratum, so the same model re-reading the same task gives a different depth more often than not even with the panel fixed; then App. E.2's worry ('both runs at a sufficient cap can fail and raise $D$ by a cap; such tasks may also be harder for other models, so this error could produce a correlation between $D$ and difficulty that does not come from depth') is the main effect rather than a robustness footnote, the depth-difficulty partial correlation on the paper's own tasks ($-0.29$, 95% CI $-0.53$ to $-0.02$, 52 tasks) is re-read as the measuring model's failure rate, and the ruler needs $n_r \approx 7$ runs at the boundary cap before any dataset is called shallow or deep. Either way the result changes a ruler: if P1-P3 hold, 'depth' joins the lane's list of quantities that are properties of the protocol until the panel is named (temperature-0 determinism, the per-turn luck term), and every 'report depth alongside work' recommendation acquires a panel clause and a $\Phi$; if the field's cell holds, the paper's recommendation gets its missing certificate and a two-run replicate rule is enough.

identifiability: Random given: the task (instruction, Docker image, verifier $V$ and start state $e_0$ fixed), the harness (terminus-2 multi-segment, 150-turn uncapped limit, 30-minute agent limit on existing tasks, 10,000-byte output truncation, 60-second per-command wait), the cap text appended verbatim from App. B, the model and its serving provider, and the sampling temperature. The pass bit $X_{\tau m T r}$ is a verifier output (deterministic check scripts, App. F), never a judge. Whose temperature: the measuring models', at provider defaults in the paper ('keep the default of the provider for the other models', App. I; the default is not stated, so the paper's run residual is at an unknown temperature); the probe pins the temperature, reports it, and runs a temperature-0 arm on 10 tasks per model to split $\sigma^2(\epsilon)$ into sampling and serving-plus-timing parts (a run at temperature 0 that still varies is the serving stack's arithmetic and the environment's clock, the lane's own earlier finding). Whose property: $D$ is a property of the design (task, panel, harness, cap grid, protocol); the G-study says what share is the task's. The cap grid is the measurement scale and is declared a fixed facet; the harness is a hidden fixed facet in both the paper and the probe (one harness), so the probe's $\sigma^2(\tau)$ still contains the task-by-harness interaction and the record says so; a second harness is the next D-study, not this one. The min over models is not a mean: the probe reports the four-model min for comparability with the paper and the panel-mean $\bar y_{\tau \cdot}$ as the G-theory quantity, and names the panel. Censoring: a (task, model) cell with no pass at any cap has no $y$; censoring is informative (correlated with depth), so components are estimated within strata and the censoring rate is a reported quantity, with the kill clause below if it exceeds 40% in a stratum. No luck term is asserted: the environment after a command is deterministic up to timing; the run variance is the sampler's and the clock's.

probe.design: Step 1 (2 days, $0): fix the 60-task panel from the paper's released task lists (App. C sampling rules; TB2, TW, RST and FACET tasks are public; the paper's own 105 tasks if the header's Dataset link resolves), build the terminus-2 multi-segment harness with the App. B cap text and limits, pin providers and temperature. Step 2 (3 days wall clock, about $1,000 of API calls, 0 GPU-hours, about 500 container-hours of CPU): 60 tasks x 4 models x 8 caps x 4 runs = 7,680 capped runs, 32 containers in parallel; billed input tokens dominate (a 45-turn run re-reads about 30k tokens per turn; prefix caching on DeepSeek and GLM cuts the bill), estimate 2.2B input tokens at $0.15-0.30 per million plus 10% output. Step 3 (1 day): temperature-0 arm, 10 tasks per model at the two boundary caps, 4 runs each (320 runs). Step 4 (1 day): components by stratum, $E\rho^2$ and $\Phi$ for the released design and the two-model min, $A$, $L$, $C$, the certificate run count per stratum from the $\hat p_{\tau m D^-}$ distribution, bootstrap over tasks. Optional step 5 (about $300): one frontier model (GPT-6.1 Sol) on the deep stratum only, to see whether the panel-min keeps falling with a stronger merger.
probe.dollars: about $1,000 of API calls at Flash-class prices (2.2B billed input tokens, 10% output) plus about $300 for the optional frontier arm; container compute about 500 CPU-hours on spot instances, under $50
probe.days: 7 days: 2 of harness and panel work, 3 of runs, 1 for the temperature-0 arm, 1 of analysis
probe.kills_if: Dead as a claim if, in both strata above the floor, $\Phi \ge 0.8$ for the single-model two-run label, $A \ge 0.85$, $L \le 0.1$ and $C \le 0.15$ with bootstrap intervals excluding the P1-P3 thresholds: the depth label is a task property to within one grid level and the import is a footnote ('report $\Phi$ and the panel') that 2611.01927's authors would add in a revision. Dead as a ruler if the censoring rate (no pass at any cap for a (task, model) pair) exceeds 40% in a stratum, because the G-study then has no balanced cells and the right instrument is a censored-survival model of the cap-to-pass, a different import; or if the temperature-0 arm reproduces the temperature-default label disagreement (then $\sigma^2(\epsilon)$ is the serving stack's and the environment clock's, and the result belongs to the L1 determinism thread, not to depth). Also a footnote and not a paper if $L$ and $C$ meet their thresholds only through MiMo and Qwen having higher $D$ than DeepSeek everywhere (a pure model main effect with no interaction), which is the 'field assumes' cell with a shift.
probe.cheapest_probe: Steps 1, 2 and 4 alone; the temperature-0 arm is $40 and settles the ruler clause, so it stays in.

consumers.class: Builders of synthetic terminal-task datasets who will adopt the paper's recommendation to 'report depth alongside work' (TMax, SETA, RST, FACET, TerminalWorld; the Depth pipeline's own release)
consumers.action_changed: Report $D$ with its model panel named as a fixed facet, the replicate count at the boundary caps, and $\Phi$ for the deep / shallow cut; label a task 'deep' only when the certificate holds; stop quoting a panel-min as a task fact.

consumers.class: Benchmark owners who ship difficulty or horizon labels (Terminal-Bench author ratings, TerminalWorld difficulty fields, METR human-time baselines and HCAST, the paper's audited '$D \le 3$' shares)
consumers.action_changed: Add a reliability column to the label (a dependability index from replicated readings) the way scores now carry run counts; allocate the label's replicates by Neyman's rule to the boundary cells, not uniformly.

consumers.class: Training teams that select tasks by a depth or horizon label for SFT or RL curricula (the paper's sec. 4.6 SFT on its deep tasks; L2 long-horizon RL groups buying 'deep' data)
consumers.action_changed: Select on the panel-mean or certified label, because selecting on a two-model min selects the measuring models' merging failures (regression to the mean on the curriculum) and the curriculum's 'depth' is partly the cheap models' habits.

consumers.class: Agent psychometrics and evaluation-design groups (2604.00594, 2610.12466, 2608.00355 on item difficulty; 2512.06710 on ICC for scores; the W43 G-theory records 2610.00651 and 2608.11323)
consumers.action_changed: Treat protocol-defined labels (depth, time horizon, difficulty tier) as measurements with facets before using them as item covariates or difficulty anchors; test a label's invariance across model panels the way DIF is tested across examinee groups.

papers.title: Stochasticity in Agentic Evaluations: Quantifying Inconsistency with Intraclass Correlation
papers.trick: Run each query many times and report the intraclass correlation, the share of score variance that is between queries rather than between repeated runs of the same query, so a leaderboard gain counts only if the ICC also rises; ICC 0.30-0.77 on GAIA, converging by 8-32 trials.
papers.did_not_do: The object is the query and the reliability is the score's: 'ICC decomposes observed variance into between-query variance (task difficulty) and within-query variance (agent inconsistency)', one model at a time; task difficulty is the universe-score component by assumption, never a label whose own facets (model, cap, harness) are tested; no min-over-facet estimator, no cut-score dependability, no horizon or depth label, GAIA and FRAMES rather than terminal tasks, no allocation rule beyond a convergence count.

papers.title: CurveShift: Is Agent Progress Scalar? Separating Level from Shape
papers.trick: Fit one Rasch model with rising ability to METR time-horizon data and show the apparent shift of gains toward hard tasks is a ceiling effect, then isolate a small residual hard-task gain on LiveCodeBench where no scaffold confounds the model.
papers.did_not_do: Difficulty is a latent item parameter assumed the task's and invariant across models; the paper tests the shape of the difficulty-response curve, not whether a protocol-assigned label reproduces under a new model, run or harness; it names the model-scaffold confound ('newer models are usually run with newer agentic harnesses') and resolves it by leaving agents out, not by making the harness a facet; no replicate facet, no dependability index. Third: 2610.12466 (id_list) re-estimates METR time horizons with splines and item-response theory and offers 'diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity', with the human-time label taken as given and no reliability of any label. Fourth: 2604.00594 'augments Item Response Theory' with task features and 'a novel decomposition of agent ability into LLM and scaffold ability components', so the model-by-task term is modelled on the ability side and difficulty stays the item's; its promise that designers 'can better calibrate the difficulty of their new tasks without running computationally expensive agent evaluations' is the opposite direction from a replicated G-study. Fifth: 2503.14499 (id_list) labels tasks by timed human experts and 2509.09677 measures the horizon a model executes from per-step accuracy; neither abstract reports a reliability coefficient for the label, and the METR full text was not read here. Sixth, from the lane's own records: 2610.00651 and 2608.11323 (W43) apply G-theory to agent scores with the model as object, never to a task label. The card paper 2611.01927 is the only source with a protocol-defined depth label, and its reliability evidence is the one-sided App. E.1 check (25% of labels moved; 11 of 40 deep labels crossing the cut; a part-whole Spearman of 0.91) and the App. E.2 subset ($R = 1$) with no replicate of the label.

nearest.verdict: Not made. The G-theory import for agent scores is in print (2610.00651, 2608.11323; ICC in 2512.06710) and the item-response import for task difficulty is in print (2604.00594, 2603.23749, 2608.00355, 2610.12466; the W44 S5xF2 record), and both assume what this import tests: that difficulty or depth is the task's and the model is on the ability side. No fetched source decomposes a protocol-defined difficulty or horizon label into task, model, model-by-task and run components, grades its cut-score use by $\Phi$, treats the min over models as a biased extreme statistic, names the harness as a hidden fixed facet, or allocates the label's replicates to the boundary caps. Not a rename of the W43 S8xF1 record (effort-by-task interaction on scores, model as object), the W43 S6xF1 record (cost as the measured quantity), or the W46 S12xF1 record (checkpoint x problem x draw inside one training run): here the object is the task, the measured quantity is a label defined as a min over design cells, and the field's instruments that matter are $\Phi$ for absolute decisions, the fixed-facet rule for the panel and the one-sided nesting confound. Not a rename of 2611.01927's own caveat ('depends on the models, the harness'): the paper names the facets and estimates none; its 0.91 is not a reliability. Density: 1 + 23 + 14 hits in the three queries, one on-point paper (the card's), about one horizon-measurement paper a month in the window; race window about 3 months against a 7-day, $1,000 probe; solo position.

reason_for_pick: S5 is this week's live shape through card 2611.01927: a new protocol-defined horizon label ($D$, smallest stated cap that passes) audits six datasets and sells a seventh, with the paper stating that the label depends on the models and the harness and estimating no component; its one-sided second-model check moves 25% of labels above the floor and 11 of 40 'deep' existing labels across its own cut. F1 is in Jacob's evaluable set and its three earlier imports (S6xF1 cost, S8xF1 effort-by-task, S12xF1 checkpoint-by-problem) all took the model or the training run as the object of measurement; the open F1 question for this card is the task as object and a min-over-facets label as the measurement, where Brennan's absolute-decision index $\Phi$, the fixed-facet rule and the nesting confound apply directly and nobody has computed any reliability coefficient for an agent-task difficulty or horizon label (Q1: 1 hit, scores only).

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2611.01927 sec. 2 ('$D$ depends on the models, the harness and the single state $e_0$, so it is an estimate rather than a bound'), sec. 3.1 ('a model that merges poorly overestimates the depth'), App. E.2 ('this error could produce a correlation between $D$ and difficulty that does not come from depth'), sec. 5 (builders should 'report depth alongside work'); 2512.06710 ('reporting a single accuracy number from a single run, obscures the variance'); 2608.00355 ('a gain on hard tasks cannot be assigned to the model or its scaffold'); 2610.12466 ('diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity'). Who pays: every dataset that will ship a depth column, every benchmark that ships a difficulty or horizon label, every training team buying 'deep' tasks by that label.

scorecard.density_and_ownership: Occupied: G-theory and ICC for agent scores with the model as object (2610.00651, 2608.11323, 2512.06710); item-response difficulty for agent tasks with difficulty on the item and ability split into LLM and scaffold (2604.00594, 2603.23749), Rasch on METR data (2608.00355), IRT re-estimation of time horizons with construct-validity plots (2610.12466); the depth label itself and its one-sided model check (2611.01927, 2026-11-01). Unoccupied in every fetched source: a facet decomposition of any protocol-defined difficulty or horizon label, $\Phi$ for its cut-score use, the extreme-statistic reading of a min over models, the harness as a hidden fixed facet, Neyman replicates at boundary caps. Natural first movers: the 2611.01927 authors (they own the harness, the 105 tasks and the run logs; a revision adding more models is the cheapest version and the re-open test is asking them), the ICC authors (they own the vocabulary and a public code base), the METR and 2610.12466 groups for time-horizon labels. Race window: about one horizon-measurement paper a month in Q2's window, none on label reliability; 7-day probe; solo position with public tasks and API models.
scorecard.why_now: 2611.01927 (2026-11-01) is the first protocol-defined depth label and recommends that every builder report it, while its own App. E.1 and E.2 supply the one-sided facet sizes (25% of labels, 11 of 40 deep labels, both-runs-fail at $(1-p)^2$) that make the G-study's expected ordering a pre-registrable bet; Flash-class models at $0.15-0.30 per million input tokens with fixed providers put 7,680 capped runs at about $1,000; the W43-W46 F1 records already carried the variance-components vocabulary into the lane for scores, so the task-as-object version is the field's next step and the only one left.
scorecard.register_and_what_it_is_not: Measurement register: a G-study of an existing ruler on public tasks, with a mechanism (unmerged turns are model-specific) and a consequence each way (panel clause and $\Phi$ with seven boundary runs; or a certificate that two runs suffice). It is not a new depth measure, not a construction-time key-step count (that is the card's information_asymmetry inference, a separate probe), not an IRT model of difficulty, not a repeat of the S8xF1, S6xF1 or S12xF1 designs, and not a critique of the paper's generation pipeline or SFT result.

title: A success checker is a block-spin map from the simulator microstate to one bit, read at a persistence window and a tolerance that nobody names: scan the window on frozen RoboTwin rollouts under a repeat run, a halved time step, a doubled contact offset and injected inference latency, and sort each setting into relevant or irrelevant by whether its excess flip rate decays to the repeat floor as the window grows
abstract: In statistical physics the macroscopic description of a system is a coarse-graining, a map from the microstate to a few kept variables, and two results govern it. The renormalization group sorts microscopic perturbations by what happens to their effect as the scale grows: a perturbation whose magnitude 'always increases' as 'the scale of the system goes from small to large' is relevant and 'is needed to describe the macroscopic behavior of the system'; one that 'always decreases' is irrelevant and is 'not needed'; the differences between microscopically different systems 'are determined by irrelevant observables' (Wikipedia, Renormalization group, sec. 'Relevant and irrelevant operators' and 'Critical exponents and universality', raw wikitext fetched 2026-11-22). The Kemeny-Snell lumpability condition says when a partition of the state space is itself a Markov description: for any two blocks $t_i, t_j$ and any two microstates $n, n'$ in $t_i$, $\sum_{m \in t_j} p(n, m) = \sum_{m \in t_j} p(n', m)$, the probability of leaving the block must not depend on which microstate inside it the system occupies (Wikipedia, Lumpability, sec. 'Definition', fetched 2026-11-22). A benchmark's success checker is exactly such a map: $c : \mathcal{X} \to \{0, 1\}$ sends the simulator microstate $x_t$ (every body pose and velocity, the contact set the engine reports, the commanded and actual gripper state) to one bit, and the recorded episode verdict is $C_\tau = \mathbf{1}[\exists\, t : c(x_s) = 1 \ \forall s \in [t, t + \tau]]$ at a persistence window $\tau$ (the shipped readout is $\tau = 0$, first hit, with the episode terminated there; SimAudit's Verified checker is $\tau = 1\,\mathrm{s}$; judging the terminal state is $\tau \to T$). This week's two cards are failures of the two physics conditions stated in robotics words. 2611.25179 (SimAudit): a stack that passes the checker and 'Within 60 ms, the stack is falling', a gripper checker that 'turns true on the first physics step after the open command, with the fingers still closed on the object', a contact point reported 'across an air gap of up to 2 cm', and early termination that credits a policy that stops ('The recorded episode is the same in both cases', App. C) are microstates inside the block $A_1 = c^{-1}(1)$ whose escape probability differs from the true successes' escape probability: the partition is not lumpable, so the bit carries memory of the microstate, and 61 defects in 49 of 142 tasks flip 3.1-5.6% of RoboTwin episodes (Table 2) under a repair that is, in physics terms, a longer window plus a force condition. 2611.26969 (RoboDyna): advancing the simulator during the policy's forward pass (109-236 ms against a 60 ms control interval) flips 85 / 63 / 34 of 700 paired seeded episodes (12.1 / 9.0 / 4.9%) while the mean success rate moves at most 0.03, and the field reads that as latency sensitivity without the repeat-run null that a relevant-operator test requires. Carried into L5, the import says: treat the persistence window $\tau$ and the spatial tolerance of the checker as the coarse-graining scale, treat each simulator setting (physics step $h$, contact offset $d_c$, injected latency $\delta$) as a microscopic perturbation, and measure the excess flip rate $\psi_j(\tau) = \phi_j(\tau) - \phi_0(\tau)$, where $\phi_j(\tau)$ is the share of paired seeded episodes whose verdict $C_\tau$ differs between the shipped setting and the perturbed one and $\phi_0(\tau)$ is the same share between two runs at the shipped setting (the repeat null). A setting is irrelevant to the recorded success bit at the readout scale where $\psi_j(\tau)$ has decayed to the floor, relevant where it has not; the exponent $y_j = -\,\mathrm{d} \ln \psi_j / \mathrm{d} \ln \tau$ over $\tau \in \{60\,\mathrm{ms}, 250\,\mathrm{ms}, 1\,\mathrm{s}, 3\,\mathrm{s}\}$ is the sorting statistic, positive for irrelevant. The pre-registered surprise (judgment probabilities): expected 0.45, on RoboTwin frozen rollouts the time step and the transient-success operators are irrelevant by $\tau = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ ($\psi_h < 1$ pp on at least 7 of 10 tasks) while they are not at the shipped $\tau = 0$ ($\psi_h > 2$ pp), the air-gap contact operator is flat in $\tau$ (a spatial operator a time window cannot remove), and latency is relevant on the dynamic tasks ($\psi_\delta > 3$ pp at every $\tau$), so one window both repairs the checker and makes the numerics irrelevant, which no one has said; the field assumes 0.30, the numerics are a detail at every $\tau$ ($\psi_h \approx \psi_{d_c} \approx 0$ at $\tau = 0$ too) and the latency flips are all signal ($\phi_0 \approx 0$); belief-changing 0.25, either the repeat floor $\phi_0$ is itself 3-6% at every $\tau$ (the success bit is not a slow variable of the simulator on contact-rich tasks at any readout scale, so SimAudit's 3-6% and RoboDyna's 5-12% are the same floor measured twice and no checker repair at fixed settings fixes it) or the time step is relevant at $\tau = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ (the Verified checkers are repaired at one setting only and checker validity cannot be certified without naming the numerics). Position both: the RoboTwin arm is solo (released checkers, released policies, SAPIEN); the RoboDyna arm needs the checkpoints. About 85 GPU-hours, about $250, 10 days; the window and tolerance scans are offline on logged states.

sentences: A coarse-graining sorts the details it drops by what the scale does to them: 'For a certain observable $A$ of a physical system undergoing an RG transformation, the magnitude of the observable as the scale of the system goes from small to large determines the importance of the observable for the scaling law': if it 'always increases' the observable is 'relevant', if it 'always decreases' it is 'irrelevant', otherwise 'marginal'; 'A relevant observable is needed to describe the macroscopic behavior of the system; irrelevant observables are not needed', and 'Most observables are irrelevant, i.e., the macroscopic physics is dominated by only a few observables in most systems' (Wikipedia, Renormalization group, sec. 'Relevant and irrelevant operators').

Why microscopically different systems share a macroscopic outcome: 'the differences in phenomena among the individual fine-scale components are determined by irrelevant observables, while the relevant observables are shared in common', so macroscopic behaviour falls into 'a small set of universality classes, specified by the shared sets of relevant observables' (same page, sec. 'Critical exponents and universality'); the coarse-graining step itself is Kadanoff's 1966 'block-spin' transformation, in which blocks of microscopic spins are replaced by one variable and the couplings are followed as the block size grows (same page, History and 'Simple model: block spins').

A partition of a state space is a valid coarse description of a Markov process only when it is lumpable: 'A continuous-time Markov chain $\{X_i\}$ is lumpable with respect to the partition $T$ if and only if, for any subsets $t_i$ and $t_j$ in the partition, and for any states $n, n'$ in subset $t_i$, $\sum_{m \in t_j} q(n, m) = \sum_{m \in t_j} q(n', m)$, where $q(i, j)$ is the transition rate from state $i$ to state $j$' (and the same with transition probabilities $p(n, m)$ for a stochastic matrix); when the condition holds the lumped matrix $P_t$ is itself a Markov chain on the blocks, and when it fails the block process depends on which microstate inside the block the system occupies (Wikipedia, Lumpability, sec. 'Definition', Kemeny and Snell 1960 p. 124; 'quasi-lumpability' is the case where 'a small change in the rate matrix makes the chain lumpable', Franceschinis and Muntz 1993).
